title: All the decoder ever sees
insight: This one line, on 2010-03-24, is the model's entire input. No labels, no appliance list.

explain.what: Total household power for one unseen day, one reading per minute.
explain.how: Taken straight from the meter column of the dataset. Nothing is smoothed.
explain.read: Flat stretches are the home idling. Sudden square jumps usually mean something switched on or off.
explain.where: Every smart meter records a line like this. Utilities use it for billing and for grid planning.

title: Four years, split by time
insight: 1,358 complete days. Everything from 2009 on is unseen: 650 test days.

explain.what: Total energy per day across the whole dataset.
explain.how: Sum of each day's minute readings divided by 60. Only complete days are kept, and the split is by date, never shuffled.
explain.read: The yearly wave is the seasons. The model learns from the left part and is scored only on the right part.
explain.where: Time-ordered splits are the standard defence against leakage in forecasting and sensor work.

title: Power readings pile up at certain levels
insight: Half of all minutes are at or below 0.59 kW, yet the top reading reaches 11.1 kW.

explain.what: How often each power level occurs across training minutes, on a log scale.
explain.how: A histogram with 0.1 kW bins. The vertical axis is logarithmic so rare high loads stay visible.
explain.read: Bumps are levels the house often sits at. Mixed peaks like these are why one Gaussian cannot describe the data.
explain.where: Multi-peak histograms are the classic sign that a hidden-state or mixture model is needed.

title: When the house uses power, by month
insight: Evening peaks are strongest in winter. The summer dip shows up in almost every hour.

explain.what: Average power for each hour of the day in each calendar month.
explain.how: Group all days by month, then average by hour.
explain.read: Brighter means more power. Read across for the day's shape and down for the seasons.
explain.where: Utilities read the same pattern to plan peak capacity and time-of-day tariffs.

title: The answer key: where the energy really went
insight: Sub-meters say water heater + AC used 35.7% of all energy. The models never see these meters.

explain.what: Share of total energy recorded by each sub-meter across all days.
explain.how: Sub-meter totals divided by total energy. 'Everything else' is whatever no sub-meter covered.
explain.read: These are the true values that the decoder's guesses are checked against after training.
explain.where: Sub-metering is the expensive way to get this breakdown. Decoding tries to avoid that hardware.

title: Every switch-on leaves a jump
insight: The sizes of upward jumps give the training its label-free starting guess for each device's wattage.

explain.what: How large the minute-to-minute upward jumps in total power are.
explain.how: Differences of consecutive readings, keeping only rises above 0.15 kW, grouped by 1-D k-means.
explain.read: A bump near a size suggests a device of that size. The dashed line marks the true 1.08 kW heater step, added afterwards for checking.
explain.where: Step detection is the oldest idea in appliance monitoring and is still a common first stage.

title: Markov chain: next reading given this one
insight: The bright diagonal says the house tends to stay put: average chance of staying in a level is 82%.

explain.what: A first-order Markov chain over 12 power levels. Each row is a probability distribution over next minute's level.
explain.how: Count each move between levels in the training days, add one to every cell, then divide each row by its total.
explain.read: Row = this minute, column = next minute. Brighter cells are more likely moves.
explain.where: The same counting estimator is used for text prediction, web-page ranking and weather-state models.

title: How fast the chain forgets
insight: Raising the matrix to the power k asks where you will be k minutes on. It is within 5% of the long-run mix by k = 240 minutes.

explain.what: Worst-case distance between the k-step distribution and the chain's stationary distribution.
explain.how: Compute A to the power k. Compare each row with the stationary distribution, which is the left eigenvector of A with eigenvalue 1, using total variation.
explain.read: Falling towards zero means the starting level no longer matters.
explain.where: Mixing time is a core property behind PageRank and MCMC samplers.

title: Which model explains unseen days best?
insight: The plain HMM fits best but needs 287 parameters. The factorial model uses 29, and its parameters mean something physical.

explain.what: Average log density per minute on held-out training-era days, for four models. Higher is better.
explain.how: Each model scores the same days. Discrete models are converted to densities by dividing by bin width so they can be compared.
explain.read: The jump from the first bar to the second is the value of knowing the previous reading.
explain.where: Held-out likelihood is the standard way to compare generative models when no labels exist.

title.text: Log density per minute (higher is better)

title: Can the models imitate the real memory?
insight: Real power stays correlated for hours: 0.47 at one hour. The fitted HMM forgets faster (0.24). It has no clock, so daily routine is invisible to it.

explain.what: How strongly a reading predicts one k minutes later, for real data and for data generated by each trained model.
explain.how: Sample 80 synthetic days from each model, then compute the autocorrelation at each lag for real and generated days.
explain.read: A model line below the real line has less memory than the house. The gap at long lags comes from daily routine, which these models do not represent.
explain.where: Sampling from a fitted model and comparing statistics is a standard model check.

title: Baum-Welch only climbs
insight: EM's guarantee, visible: log-likelihood never fell across any model in this run.

explain.what: Training log-likelihood per minute after each EM iteration.
explain.how: E-step: forward-backward gives expected state counts. M-step: re-estimate parameters from those counts. Repeat.
explain.read: Each curve should rise and then flatten. A fall would mean a bug in the code.
explain.where: Baum-Welch trains HMMs in speech recognition, gene finding and activity recognition.

title: Same number of states, far fewer parameters
insight: A 16-state factorial model has 29 parameters. A 16-state plain HMM has 287.

explain.what: Held-out fit against the number of hidden combinations, for the plain and factorial models.
explain.how: Each model is trained on the same days and scored on the same held-out days.
explain.read: The plain HMM's transition table grows with the square of its states. The factorial model only needs two rates per device, so its fit is a little lower.
explain.where: Factorising a large state space is the idea behind dynamic Bayesian networks.

title: BIC keeps asking for more levels
insight: BIC is lowest at the largest size tried, 16 levels. With this much data its penalty barely bites.

explain.what: Bayesian Information Criterion for plain HMMs of different sizes.
explain.how: BIC = -2 x log-likelihood + parameters x log(number of readings). Lower is better.
explain.read: A curve that keeps falling means the criterion has not found a natural size.
explain.where: BIC and AIC are the default size selectors for mixture models and HMMs.

title: What the plain HMM's levels look like
insight: 16 Gaussians, weighted by how often each state occurs, reproduce the shape of the readings.

explain.what: The real distribution of power against the distribution implied by the trained HMM.
explain.how: Weights come from the stationary distribution of A. Each state contributes one Gaussian with its learned mean and variance.
explain.read: A close match means the emissions fit. Note that no state here means 'heater': each is a level of the whole house.
explain.where: Gaussian emissions are the textbook choice for continuous HMM observations.

title: The plain HMM's learned transition table
insight: A 16 x 16 table: 240 free numbers, none of which tells you what any appliance is doing.

explain.what: Learned transition probabilities between the plain HMM's states, ordered by mean power.
explain.how: Baum-Welch re-estimates each cell as expected moves from i to j divided by expected visits to i.
explain.read: A bright diagonal means states last. Off-diagonal cells show which levels connect.
explain.where: Reading transition tables is how analysts interpret fitted HMMs.

title: Live estimate against the whole-day estimate
insight: Using the future changes F1 only from 0.795 to 0.804, but cuts on/off flicker from 28 to 17 flips a day.

explain.what: The heater chain's probability of being on, from the forward pass alone and from forward-backward.
explain.how: Filtering uses readings up to now, alpha. Smoothing also uses later readings, gamma, which is proportional to alpha x beta.
explain.read: The whole-day line is steadier because later readings can overrule a brief blip.
explain.where: Live monitoring can only filter. Overnight billing analysis can smooth.

title: Four ways to tell the same day's story
insight: Across unseen days, Viterbi and minute-by-minute decoding score the same F1 (0.805 and 0.804). The real device flips 23 times a day.

explain.what: When the heater chain is judged on, by each method, against the sub-meter.
explain.how: Whole-day probability takes the most likely state each minute. Viterbi finds the single most likely path in the log domain. Live uses only past readings.
explain.read: Orange means on. Compare each row with the top row.
explain.where: Viterbi decodes phone signals, speech and DNA. Posterior decoding is preferred when per-position accuracy matters.

title: Why the forward pass must be scaled
insight: Left unscaled, the running product leaves the range of a floating-point number (overflow) at minute 577. Scaled and log-domain answers agree to 1.8e-11.

explain.what: Size of the unscaled forward product over one real day, next to the log-likelihood from the scaled recursion.
explain.how: Unscaled: multiply as the textbook writes it. Scaled: normalise alpha each minute, keep the factor c, and use log p(x) = sum of log c.
explain.read: The line stops where a float gives up. Narrow Gaussians have densities above 1, so here it runs away upward, not down to zero.
explain.where: Every practical HMM library scales or works in logs for this reason.

title: Sum-product is forward-backward
insight: General message passing on the factor graph matches forward-backward to 3.3e-16. Max-product returned the identical Viterbi path: True.

explain.what: Each state marginal from the general algorithm against the same marginal from forward-backward, on one unseen day.
explain.how: Treat the HMM as a chain-shaped factor graph, then pass sum messages (marginals) or max messages (best path) along its edges.
explain.read: Every point on the diagonal means the two methods agree.
explain.where: The same rule powers error-correcting codes, Kalman filters and belief propagation.

title: How many devices should it look for?
insight: It keeps 4: the gain from one more chain drops by over 80% and fitting takes about 4 times longer. Answer-key scores play no part in this choice.

explain.what: Held-out fit as chains are added.
explain.how: Train with 1 to 5 chains. Stop when the next chain adds under 20% of the previous chain's gain.
explain.read: Look for where the curve flattens. Likelihood keeps rising, so a stopping rule has to be chosen.
explain.where: Choosing latent structure by held-out likelihood is common wherever labels are unavailable.

title: Different starting guesses, same answer?
insight: 5 of 7 runs put a device within 3% of the true 1.08 kW. Runs that did not landed on a much lower likelihood, and that is what rejects them.

explain.what: Wattages learned from different starting guesses.
explain.how: Start EM from the jump sizes, and from six random scalings of them. Keep the run with the highest training likelihood.
explain.read: Dots stacked in columns mean runs agree. The dashed line is the true heater, added only for checking.
explain.where: EM finds local optima, so random restarts are standard practice.

title: One line, unmixed
insight: The coloured layers are the model's explanation of 2010-03-24. The white line is the total it was given.

explain.what: Each discovered device's expected power through a typical unseen day.
explain.how: P(device on) from forward-backward, times that device's learned wattage, stacked on the always-on level.
explain.read: Where layers follow the white line, the story explains the reading. Short spikes it does not cover are devices it has no chain for.
explain.where: This is the output of non-intrusive load monitoring. Companies sell it as an energy report.

title: Opening the answer key
insight: The filled area is the real sub-meter, which the model never saw. The line is the chain it found alone.

explain.what: The heater sub-meter against the matching chain for one typical day.
explain.how: Sub-meter Wh per minute x 60 / 1000 gives kW. The chain's line is P(on) x learned wattage.
explain.read: Matching blocks mean correct detection. Gaps between the two are real mistakes, left visible.
explain.where: Blind validation like this separates a real discovery from a model that merely fits.

title: It found 1.079 kW. The real one is 1.08 kW.
insight: Learned from the total alone: 1.079 kW. The sub-meter's most common on-power: 1.08 kW.

explain.what: The true distribution of heater-meter power when on, with the model's learned wattage marked.
explain.how: Sub-meter readings come in steps of 60 W, so the bars are spaced. The dashed line is the chain's wattage from EM.
explain.read: The line should sit on the tallest bar, and it does. This is the project's central check.
explain.where: Recovering a physical constant from indirect data is the strongest evidence a latent model is real.

title: Does each chain match a real meter?
insight: Only the heater gets a clean match, F1 0.80. Kitchen and laundry peak at 0.38 and 0.28: those appliances stay mixed together.

explain.what: F1 score of each chain against each sub-meter on unseen days.
explain.how: Mark a chain 'on' when P(on) > 0.5 and compare with the sub-meter's on/off state. Chains are matched to meters on validation days, not test days.
explain.read: One bright cell per row would mean clean separation. The bottom two rows show where this fails.
explain.where: Blind source separation studies report the same kind of confusion table.

title: Heater energy by month: guess against truth
insight: Over 650 unseen days the model estimated 5,796 kWh against 6,574 kWh real (-11.8%). Monthly correlation r = 0.91.

explain.what: Average heater energy per day for each unseen month.
explain.how: Estimated = sum of P(on) x wattage / 60. True = sub-meter total / 1000.
explain.read: The two lines should rise and fall together. The gap between them is the bias.
explain.where: Monthly appliance breakdowns are what utility energy reports show customers.

title: Heater energy, one dot per day
insight: Day-level correlation r = 0.83, with an average miss of 1.8 kWh a day.

explain.what: Each unseen day's estimated heater energy against its true value.
explain.how: Same formulas as the monthly chart, without averaging.
explain.read: Dots on the dashed line are perfect. A cloud below it means the model under-counts.
explain.where: Parity plots are the standard way to inspect a regression-type estimate.

title: The bill, split by discovered device
insight: The device matched to the heater takes 34.9% of the total. The sub-meter says 39.6%.

explain.what: Share of total energy attributed to each discovered device on unseen days.
explain.how: Device kWh = sum of P(on) x wattage / 60. Unexplained = total minus everything the model accounts for.
explain.read: This is what the app turns into rupees. The model does not name devices; the answer key names one of them after training.
explain.where: The appliance-level bill is the main consumer use of load monitoring.

title: Where the HMM's assumption breaks
insight: An HMM can only produce a straight line here. Real on-runs average 45 minutes and the chain believes 56.

explain.what: Chance that a heater on-run lasts at least n minutes: real, decoded, and implied by the model's switching rate.
explain.how: Measure run lengths from the on/off sequences. The model's line is (1 - p_off) to the power n.
explain.read: On a log axis a geometric distribution is straight. Bends away from it are real behaviour the model cannot express.
explain.where: Hidden semi-Markov models exist to fix exactly this.

title.text: Chance of lasting at least n

title: Not every day is a good day
insight: Median day F1 0.81, worst tenth 0.64, best tenth 0.92. The app's bad-day button shows that low end.

explain.what: Distribution of the heater F1 score, computed one day at a time.
explain.how: Score each unseen day separately. Days when neither the model nor the meter sees the heater on are left out.
explain.read: A long left tail means some days are poorly explained.
explain.where: Reporting a spread stops a single average from hiding failures.

title: A week, seen only through the meter
insight: The 2.11 kW chain's midday use rises from 7% of minutes on weekdays to 18% at weekends.

explain.what: How often the largest non-heater chain is on, per hour and weekday.
explain.how: Average P(on) > 0.5 over all unseen days, grouped by weekday and hour.
explain.read: Bright cells are when the home is busy. Nobody told the model what a weekend is.
explain.where: This is the privacy concern raised in smart-meter research.

title: The same week, from the real kitchen and laundry meters
insight: Pattern correlation with the decoded chain is r = 0.69. Raw total power scores r = 0.71, so the leak is in the meter data itself, not in this model.

explain.what: How often the kitchen or laundry sub-meter is on, per hour and weekday.
explain.how: Same grouping as the previous chart, using the sub-meters.
explain.read: Compare the shapes, not the brightness. The evening peak and weekend midday show in both.
explain.where: Comparisons like this are why meter data is treated as personal data in several countries.

title: Predicting the next reading
insight: One minute ahead, nothing beats copying the last reading (error 0.239 kW). By 15 minutes the HMM leads (0.662 against 0.725).

explain.what: Prediction error against how far ahead the model looks.
explain.how: From the filtered state alpha at time t, the k-step prediction is alpha x A^k x means. Compare with what actually happened.
explain.read: Lower is better. Lines meeting the 'average day' line at long range means the current state has been forgotten.
explain.where: Short-term load forecasting uses the same logic for grid balancing.

title: The slow trend under the daily noise
insight: Learned noise: process q = 4.28, reading r = 51.3. Reading noise dominates, so the filter moves only 25% of the way towards each new day.

explain.what: Daily energy with the Kalman filter's level and the backward-smoothed level.
explain.how: Local-level model: level follows a random walk, and each day is level plus noise. EM with the RTS smoother learns q and r.
explain.read: Grey is one noisy day at a time. The filter line lags slightly. The smoother uses later days, so it does not lag.
explain.where: Kalman filters run in navigation, tracking, economics and sensor fusion.

title: Missing days widen the band on their own
insight: A 6-day outage: with no readings the model only predicts, so its uncertainty grows until data returns. 82 days are missing or incomplete in total.

explain.what: Filter level with a two-standard-deviation band around the longest gap.
explain.how: On a missing day, run the predict step (variance + q) and skip the update.
explain.read: A wider band means less certainty. It snaps back within days of data returning.
explain.where: Handling dropouts without special cases is a major practical advantage of state-space models.

title: The gain settles quickly
insight: It settles at 0.250. In steady state this filter behaves like a moving average with a learned weight, which is why it shows no speed advantage in the slow-decline test.

explain.what: Kalman gain over the first 90 days.
explain.how: Gain = predicted variance / (predicted variance + r). Breaks in the line are missing days, which have no update.
explain.read: A large gain trusts new data while the level is uncertain. It flattens quickly, and jumps briefly after a gap because uncertainty grew.
explain.where: Steady-state gains make Kalman filters cheap enough for embedded hardware.

title: EM learns the two noise levels
insight: The likelihood rises at every step, which is checked by a test in the repository.

explain.what: Training log-likelihood after each EM iteration for the linear dynamical system.
explain.how: E-step: filter and RTS smoother. M-step: closed-form updates for q and r.
explain.read: Rises and flattens. It climbs slowly near the top, which is why training runs to convergence instead of a fixed short count. A dip would indicate a bug.
explain.where: EM for state-space models is used whenever noise levels cannot be measured directly.

title: Predicting tomorrow's total
insight: Kalman 6.11 kWh against a plain 7-day average 6.11 kWh: effectively level. Both clearly beat 'same as yesterday' at 7.56.

explain.what: One-day-ahead error on unseen days.
explain.how: Kalman uses the predicted level. The others use the rule named on each bar.
explain.read: Lower is better.
explain.where: These simple rules are the benchmarks any forecasting model should have to beat.

title: Tried and not better: spotting a slow decline
insight: Injected 40% decline over 8 weeks: Kalman alarms at 45 days, 7-day average at 45. False alarms are high for both (40% and 38%) because seasons also shift use.

explain.what: Median days until each method raises an alarm for a simulated slow decline.
explain.how: Reduce consumption gradually from a chosen day. Raise an alarm when the signal falls 3 standard deviations below the previous 60 days. The decline is simulated, not real.
explain.read: Shorter is better. The bars are close, so the Kalman filter gives no real detection advantage here.
explain.where: Change-point monitoring would need a seasonal model first. This is reported as a negative result.

title: Is the heater on this minute? Everyone's score
insight: With labels, CART, depth 8 wins at 0.919. With no labels, the decoder scores 0.805 against 0.482 for the best threshold. Labels help, and they require extra hardware.

explain.what: F1 on 650 unseen days for every method.
explain.how: All methods predict on/off each minute on the same days. Thresholds and trees learn on training-era days only.
explain.read: Orange methods see only the total. Blue methods also learned from the real sub-meter.
explain.where: Benchmarks against simple baselines stop complex models from being adopted without reason.

title: Precision and recall
insight: The no-label thresholds are precise but miss most of the heater's minutes. The decoder keeps the precision and finds far more of them.

explain.what: Each method's precision against its recall on unseen days.
explain.how: Precision = correct 'on' calls / all 'on' calls. Recall = correct 'on' calls / all real 'on' minutes.
explain.read: Top right is best. Hover a dot for its method.
explain.where: Precision and recall matter when 'on' is the minority, as it is here.

title: Sequence models do not flicker
insight: The real heater switches 23 times a day. CART, looking at each minute on its own, reports 39. The whole-day decoder reports 17.

explain.what: On/off changes per day for each method.
explain.how: Count how often the predicted state changes, averaged across days.
explain.read: Closer to the dashed line is more realistic. Too many means phantom switching.
explain.where: Hidden Markov smoothing is often added after per-frame classifiers for this reason.

title: Energy total, per method
insight: The decoder under-counts by 11.9%. Rule-based energy estimates can look close while being wrong minute by minute.

explain.what: Percentage error in total heater energy on unseen days.
explain.how: Estimated total against the sub-meter total. Rivals using on/off multiply on-minutes by the average on-power seen in training.
explain.read: Closer to zero is better, but errors can cancel, so read this next to the F1 chart.
explain.where: Billing estimates care about the total, while control systems care about timing.

title: How many labelled days until a tree wins?
insight: A decision tree passes the decoder with about 3 days of real sub-meter labels. That is the honest price of 'no labels': zero hardware, some accuracy.

explain.what: CART's F1 on unseen days against how many days of sub-meter labels it trained on.
explain.how: Random subsets of training days, four repeats each, averaged. The dashed line is the decoder, which uses none.
explain.read: Where the line crosses the dashes is where labelling starts to pay off. It would need redoing for every home.
explain.where: Learning curves like this guide decisions on how much labelling to pay for.

title: Tree depth and overfitting
insight: Validation peaks at depth 8, which is what gets used on the unseen days.

explain.what: Training and validation F1 as the tree is allowed to grow deeper.
explain.how: Grow by Gini impurity, choosing the best split over quantile-binned features.
explain.read: A widening gap between the lines means the tree is memorising training minutes.
explain.where: Depth is CART's main complexity control.

title: AdaBoost, round by round
insight: Reaches F1 0.874 on validation after 60 small trees.

explain.what: Boosted ensemble F1 as weak learners are added.
explain.how: Each round reweights the minutes the ensemble got wrong, fits a depth-2 tree, and adds it with weight alpha = 0.5 ln((1-err)/err).
explain.read: Rising lines mean each tree adds something. A falling validation line would mean overfitting.
explain.where: Boosting and its descendants lead on many tabular problems.

title: How much each small tree gets to vote
insight: Early trees get the biggest votes. Later ones focus on the hard minutes and count for less.

explain.what: The weight alpha assigned to each weak learner.
explain.how: Alpha is computed from each tree's weighted error, so a more accurate tree gets a larger vote.
explain.read: A falling curve is normal.
explain.where: This additive weighting is AdaBoost's defining step.

title: What the tree looks at
insight: Its most-used features are 'power now' (78%) and 'min over +/-5 min' (7%).

explain.what: Share of the tree's total impurity reduction attributed to each feature.
explain.how: Add up the weighted Gini gain of every split on each feature, then normalise.
explain.read: A long bar means the tree relies on that feature.
explain.where: Impurity importance is a quick way to inspect tree models, though it can favour high-cardinality features.

title: A threshold needs to know the answer
insight: The good threshold is around 1.10 kW. Without labels, 2-means and Otsu land near 1.84 kW and score poorly.

explain.what: F1 on unseen days for every possible threshold on total power.
explain.how: Sweep thresholds and score each one. Thresholds used by the rivals were chosen on training days, not read from this curve.
explain.read: The curve shows how much depends on picking the right cut-off, which needs labels.
explain.where: Threshold rules are the simplest possible baseline for any detector.

title: Decoder's mistakes, counted
insight: Misses 78,035 heater minutes and raises 53,026 false ones, out of 936,000 minutes.

explain.what: Confusion matrix for the heater chain on unseen days.
explain.how: Compare P(on) > 0.5 with the sub-meter for every minute.
explain.read: The diagonal is correct. Misses (bottom left) outnumber false alarms (top right), which matches the energy under-count.
explain.where: The basic summary behind precision, recall and F1.
